title: The Letter at the Bell
logline: When a Winchester solicitor's letter names her cousin heir to a widow's cottage, Eleanor Fenwick must wait on the one man in the parish too honest to tell her he already knows she is right.
promise: A codicil built on a borrowed name is unpicked fact by fact, a fortune hunter's debts catch up with him before the wedding he is counting on, and a husband's silence turns out to be loyalty, not deceit.
setting: Amberlight parish, Hampshire, spring 1818. Fenwick Cottage stands on the Bramdean road, half a mile past the mill cottages.

cast.name: Mrs Judith Rowe
cast.station: wife of the curate of Amberlight; no fortune of her own
cast.want: to find the truth of Mrs Fenwick's wishes without ever asking Silas to break his word
cast.appearance: Fair, freckled, of middling height, with reddish hair she cannot keep pinned and a habit of looking directly at whoever is speaking.
cast.dress: Sprigged muslin in summer, a grey wool pelisse in winter, both mended with more thrift than skill.
cast.voice_note: quiet, precise, waits a beat before answering

cast.name: Mr Silas Rowe
cast.station: curate of Amberlight; eighty a year and no expectations
cast.want: to keep a dying woman's confidence exactly as she asked, whatever it costs him at home
cast.appearance: Tall and thin, dark hair worn slightly too long, with the stoop of a man used to low doorways and a face that gives away more than he intends.
cast.dress: Worn black coat, carefully brushed, and linen that has been turned at the cuffs.
cast.voice_note: earnest, apologetic, loses the thread mid-sentence

cast.name: Mrs Honoria Pike
cast.station: widow of a naval surgeon; three hundred a year and a house on the green
cast.want: to know everything before anyone else does
cast.appearance: Short and broad, with grey hair pinned severely under a lace cap, and small quick eyes set in a round weathered face.
cast.dress: Black bombazine with a plain white fichu, ten years out of fashion and immaculately kept.
cast.voice_note: brisk, talks over people cheerfully, certain of things she has half-heard

cast.name: Miss Eleanor Fenwick
cast.station: niece and household companion to the late Mrs Martha Fenwick; expected heir to the cottage and three hundred pounds
cast.want: to keep her aunt's cottage without owing it to anyone's pity or anyone's proposal
cast.appearance: Slight and fair-haired, with a composed oval face and grey eyes that rarely leave whoever has just spoken.
cast.dress: Deep mourning black, plainly made, a single mourning ring her aunt left her.
cast.voice_note: soft-spoken, says exactly what she means and no more

cast.name: Mr Laurence Sorrel
cast.station: clerk to a Winchester firm of solicitors, sent to settle the Fenwick estate within a fortnight; a partnership awaits him if he manages it well
cast.want: to settle the estate correctly, even if it costs him the goodwill of the man his firm must rule against
cast.appearance: Tall, sandy-haired, spectacles he is forever pushing up, ink permanently at the side of one finger.
cast.dress: A serviceable brown travelling coat, creased from the coach, a leather satchel of papers always at hand.
cast.voice_note: formal at first meeting, dryly funny once he trusts you

cast.name: Mr Gerald Ashby
cast.station: cousin to the late Mrs Fenwick; a gentleman of no settled income, in debt at cards
cast.want: to secure the cottage before his card debts come due, by the codicil if it holds or by Eleanor's hand if it does not
cast.appearance: Well-built and fair, curls worn a little too fashionably long for a man of his years, a ready smile that reaches his eyes less often than it should.
cast.dress: A blue coat cut better than his purse can easily answer for.
cast.voice_note: charming, quick to laugh, quicker to change the subject

cast.name: Sally Prewitt
cast.station: maid at Fenwick Cottage these three years, in want of a character for her next place
cast.want: to tell what she saw honestly without losing the character she needs for her next place
cast.appearance: Small and quick-moving, dark hair escaping a plain cap, hands reddened from work.
cast.dress: A grey stuff gown and a clean apron, kept neat despite long hours.
cast.voice_note: flat, guarded, warms slowly once taken seriously

chapters.title: The Letter at the Bell
beats: After Mrs Martha Fenwick's burial, the Tuesday carrier leaves a Winchester solicitor's letter at the Bell, addressed to the cottage.
The landlord, busy with the coach, hands it to Mrs Pike to carry up the lane, since she is going that way already.
Mrs Pike breaks the seal 'to see it reaches the right hands' and reads it aloud to half the green: a codicil leaves the cottage to Mr Gerald Ashby, witnessed by two names nobody in the parish knows.
Miss Eleanor Fenwick, the expected heir, hears the news standing among the mourners rather than told privately.
Ashby, present at the churchyard gate, receives the news with studied modesty and is already thanking neighbours for their condolences on his loss, and his good fortune, both.

chapters.title: The Clerk on the Tuesday Coach
beats: Mr Laurence Sorrel arrives on the next Tuesday coach, sent by the Winchester firm to settle the estate within a fortnight.
He calls at the library above the draper's and meets Mrs Judith Rowe, who quietly corrects two details Mrs Pike's retelling had already gotten wrong.
Sorrel confirms the codicil, if genuine, stands: the cottage and three hundred pounds pass to Ashby, and Eleanor is left with nothing.
Ashby, met on the green, is already behaving as owner, giving instructions to the gardener and speaking warmly of Eleanor's situation.
Judith notices his warmth toward Eleanor looks less like a cousin's concern than courtship, and wonders at how quickly it has arrived.

chapters.title: What Sally Saw
beats: Judith and Silas call at the house of mourning to arrange the funeral accounts.
Sally Prewitt, the cottage maid, lets slip to Judith that Ashby left the house before nine the night the codicil is dated and did not return until after midnight.
Judith checks the solicitor's letter again: the codicil is dated ten o'clock that same evening, witnessed at the cottage itself.
Sally, afraid of losing her character if she is seen accusing a gentleman, begs Judith to keep what she has said to herself for now.
Walking home, Judith mentions the timing to Silas, who falls silent and changes the subject the moment the widow's last week is raised.

chapters.title: A Confidence Kept
beats: At home, Judith asks Silas plainly what he knows of Mrs Fenwick's last week.
He admits he holds something given him in confidence, but says he gave his word and may not speak of it unless the thing is claimed of him.
Judith does not press him further, though it plainly costs her not to.
Mrs Pike calls with news of her own: one of the codicil's two witnesses, a man named Jacob Yarrow, is known in Winchester as someone Ashby owes money to at cards.
Judith realizes the second witness's name is also one nobody local recognizes, and resolves to have Sorrel write to both.

chapters.title: The Friday Coach
beats: Sorrel writes to Jacob Yarrow asking him to confirm his signature on the codicil.
The Friday coach brings Yarrow's reply: he denies ever witnessing any such paper and demands to know why his name was used.
News of the denial reaches the library before Sorrel has finished reading it, carried accurately for once.
Ashby, undeterred, proposes to Eleanor publicly after Sunday service, calling it the surest way to settle any doubt about the cottage.
Eleanor, cornered before the whole congregation, asks only for a fortnight to consider, which Ashby grants with visible impatience.

chapters.title: The Condition
beats: Judith turns over Silas's own words, unless the thing is claimed of me, and realizes the promise carries a condition that can still be met.
She asks Sorrel to put Ashby's claim to the cottage to her husband formally, in writing, on the firm's paper, as the law allows in any dispute.
Sorrel does so, and Silas, satisfied the condition is now plainly met, produces a sealed letter Mrs Fenwick gave him weeks before her death.
With Eleanor, Sally and Sorrel gathered in the vestry, Silas breaks the seal.
The letter is Mrs Fenwick's own account: she paid Ashby's card debts in full years before, to the exact sum now claimed in the codicil, and meant the cottage for Eleanor alone.

chapters.title: The Cousin's Portion
beats: Word reaches Ashby within the hour, and he comes to the Bell demanding to see the letter for himself.
Sorrel reads aloud the sum Mrs Fenwick names, matching almost exactly what Ashby has always claimed he raised on his own credit.
Cornered, Ashby calls the letter a forgery got up against him.
Sally's account of his hours away that night, Yarrow's denial, and the widow's own seal, known to Sorrel's firm from her other papers, together break the claim.
Ashby withdraws the codicil and, quietly, asks Eleanor's forgiveness rather than her hand.

chapters.title: What Was Settled
beats: Eleanor Fenwick takes possession of the cottage and the three hundred pounds, and keeps Sally on with a proper character and better wages.
Ashby leaves Amberlight within the week; Sorrel's firm finds him honest clerking work in Winchester and nothing more.
Mrs Pike, chastened at having been wrong about so much, carries the true account of events this time without a single embellishment.
Sorrel asks Eleanor whether his firm's new agency at Amberlight might keep him settled nearby, and she allows that it might suit her too.
Walking home, Judith thanks Silas for not telling her what he knew, and he admits it was the hardest promise he has ever kept.

Tropes: The misdirected letter; The fortune hunter; The disputed inheritance.

Cast:

The central device: the late Mrs Fenwick gave Mr Rowe a sealed letter, on his promise to open it only if someone claimed the cottage against her niece in writing, to him. He is good at his work and keeps the promise even from his wife. Mrs Rowe sees that he knows something, does not ask him to break his word, works out the condition, and arranges for it to be met. Their disagreement is small and domestic, never an estrangement.

Chapter plan:
1. The Letter at the Bell — after the burial, the carrier leaves a Winchester solicitor's letter at the Bell; the landlord gives it to Mrs Pike to deliver and she reads it to half the green: a codicil leaves the cottage to Ashby, witnessed by two names nobody knows. Eleanor hears it with everyone else.
2. The Clerk on the Tuesday Coach — Sorrel arrives with a fortnight to settle; meets Mrs Rowe at the library counter over Mrs Hale; the codicil stands unless disproved; Ashby already behaves as owner and is warm toward Eleanor.
3. What Sally Saw — the Rowes call at the house of mourning; Sally says Ashby left before nine and returned after midnight, though the codicil is dated ten o'clock; Mr Rowe goes quiet on the walk home when the widow's last week comes up.
4. A Confidence Kept — at home Mrs Rowe asks him plainly; he says he gave his word and may not speak "unless the thing is claimed of me"; Mrs Pike places Yarrow as a man Ashby owes at cards.
5. The Friday Coach — Yarrow writes to Sorrel denying he witnessed anything, and Mrs Hale repeats it exactly; Ashby proposes to Eleanor publicly after Sunday service and she asks for time.
6. The Condition — Mrs Rowe works out the condition and has Sorrel put the claim to the curate in writing on the firm's paper; Mr Rowe opens the letter before Eleanor, Sally and Sorrel: the widow's own account that Ashby's portion was paid years ago, to the shilling, against his debts.
7. The Cousin's Portion — confrontation at the Bell; the sum matches what Ashby claims he raised on his own credit; he cries forgery; Sally's timing, Yarrow's letter and the widow's seal break it; he withdraws and asks Eleanor's forgiveness.
8. What Was Settled — Eleanor keeps the cottage and gives Ashby an introduction to honest work in Winchester; Mrs Pike carries the true news with unusual accuracy; Sorrel asks whether his firm's agency at Amberlight might suit Eleanor too; walking home, Mrs Rowe thanks her husband for not telling her.

Do not use: the apothecary's records or handwriting as evidence; a secret benefactor or Mrs Pike delivering money; the Hale family or any farm called Hale's Bottom; a housekeeper witness; any romance or proposal involving Mrs Rowe.
